candidates.attacker_control: An untrusted OBR repository (added via obr:url-add, or a third-party/compromised repository already configured) controls repository XML resource properties, including the resource source URI that SourceCommand reads as Resource.SOURCE_URI, and fully controls the byte content and entry names of the JAR served from that URI. The ZIP/JAR entry names are used verbatim (no URL decoding) when building filesystem paths.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: unjar does reject absolute (leading '/') entry paths and downloadSource prints an error if the destination directory does not exist (though it continues); the JAR file itself is written using only the last path segment of the URL, so the download step cannot traverse. Kar.extract already blocks '..' entries, but that guard is not shared with FileUtil. OBR commands are shell commands, so exploitation needs an authenticated/authorized user action, not a remote unauthenticated request. The source URI is expected to be consumed via the Felix bundlerepository Resource.SOURCE_URI property; I did not find any additional validation of the extracted entry names anywhere else in the OBR command package.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary file write with attacker-controlled content, anywhere the Karaf process user can write (outside the folder the operator selected). Practical impact includes overwriting configuration/startup files or scripts, or dropping artifacts into hot-deployment locations (e.g., deploy/, system repository) leading to code execution with the Karaf process privileges, plus data corruption/denial of service. Requires an interactive admin action (running obr:source -x) against a malicious repository, but the repository is exactly the untrusted input OBR is designed to consume.
candidates.prerequisites: OBR feature/bundle installed (shipped in the standard feature set): the command classes are packaged into org.apache.karaf.obr.core (obr/pom.xml Private-Package). A repository entry with a crafted source URI exists or is added. A user authorized to run obr commands executes `obr:source -x <existing-local-dir> <symbolic-name[,version]>`; the destination directory must already exist for the download to succeed.
candidates.root_cause: FileUtil.unjar validates JAR entry names only against absolute paths (entry name startsWith "/") and never rejects relative ".." path segments. For each entry, copy() resolves the entry's parent segment against the destination directory (new File(dir, destDir), then new File(targetDir, destName)), so an entry such as "../../some/dir/file" escapes the destination folder and writes to an attacker-chosen location. The sibling archive extractor in the same snapshot (Kar.extract) does contain the missing guard (entry name contains ".." or "%2e%2e" is skipped), demonstrating the intended validation that FileUtil lacks.
candidates.title: Path traversal (Zip Slip) in obr:source JAR extraction allows arbitrary file write outside the chosen directory
candidates.trace: SourceCommand.doExecute (line 43) -> resource.getProperties().get(Resource.SOURCE_URI) (line 53) -> srcURL.toURL() (line 56) -> FileUtil.downloadSource(..., extract=true) (FileUtil lines 36-94) writes the JAR into the user folder and calls unjar (lines 81-88) -> unjar (lines 96-139) rejects only names starting with "/" (lines 107-110) and passes the entry's parent segment to copy (lines 129-137) -> copy (lines 141-175) computes targetDir = new File(dir, destDir) and writes new File(targetDir, destName), resolving ".." segments outside the chosen directory. The P1 index shows the syntactic call edge SourceCommand.doExecute -> FileUtil.downloadSource and the unresolved Resource.SOURCE_URI call site, consistent with this path (index edges are navigation hints only).
candidates.unverified: Not compiled or executed; no runtime confirmation of the extraction behavior or of which repository-XML construct (source element) populates Resource.SOURCE_URI in this Felix bundlerepository version. The exact default RBAC roles required to run obr:source were not verified. Index call edges are syntactic candidates, not proof of runtime data flow.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') / Zip Slip (untrusted archive entry names)

coverage_summary: Scope filters: get_source_scope reports 1,660 model-visible files, 0 excluded by size/name/symlink, binary-like files skipped for reads; the tree contains only src/main (no src/test, manual or docs content). get_relation_scope reports the same 1,660 files indexed, index_status complete, 0 missing/mismatched, 13,906 symbols / 40,510 calls / 24,805 edges / 718 facts; qualification: static navigation candidates only, no data-flow, reachability, or exploitability proof. I inspected in detail: obr commands and util (FileUtil, SourceCommand, ObrCommandSupport), kar extraction/service, http proxy/servlet, shell core/console/security/ssh/commands, management JMX RBAC guard, jaas login modules and keystore config, service/guard proxy catalog and ACL parser, features download manager and XML/JAXB parsing, util (XmlUtils, JaasHelper, StringEscapeUtils), config, log, audit, instance, webconsole, main startup/shutdown socket, and relevant pom/feature files. Other areas (examples, archetypes, tooling, specs, assemblies) were sampled only where they document exposure (e.g., feature definitions). No code was executed and no external data was consulted.
limitations: No build, test, or execution was performed; all conclusions are source-reading based, and the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Whether the Felix bundlerepository version used here exposes the 'source' resource property from repository XML as Resource.SOURCE_URI was not verified in this snapshot; if source URIs cannot be attacker-supplied, the traversal still exists but requires a source JAR URL to be provided some other way.
The P1 index provides syntactic relations only; no complete call graph, data flow, or reachability proof, and some call sites are explicitly unresolved.
Not every one of the 1,660 files was read line by line; coverage was concentrated on security-relevant packages, so a vulnerability in an unread area cannot be excluded.
The snapshot omits all test sources, so I could not corroborate intended behavior or exploitability with tests.

The one-candidate cap means additional plausible but unconfirmed leads (listed above) were not submitted; notably the inverted redirect check in ProxyServlet may be a real defect of this snapshot, but I judged the OBR path traversal to have the only concrete high-impact security story.

rejected_leads.lead: http/src/main/java/org/apache/karaf/http/core/internal/ProxyServlet.java lines 187-198: the Location-header check is inverted (throws when the Location header IS present, then dereferences it when it is null) and lines 173-179 cast a ServletException to IOException.
rejected_leads.reason: Clearly anomalous source (likely a plant or a real fix-parent defect), but analysis shows only functional/availability impact: proxied 3xx responses cause an NPE/ClassCastException and an HTTP 500 instead of a redirect. I could not establish attacker-controlled privilege gain or data exposure, so it does not meet the concrete-security-impact bar for the single candidate slot; recorded as an unconfirmed rejecting lead.

rejected_leads.lead: kar/src/main/java/org/apache/karaf/kar/internal/Kar.java lines 115-137: '..' entries are blocked but there is no absolute-path / Windows drive-letter check on extracted entry paths ('C:/...' style).
rejected_leads.reason: Only potentially relevant on Windows layouts and only relative to the KAR storage tree; no evidence of a practical escape or of attacker-controlled input reaching it in this snapshot beyond KAR installation, which already implies trusted deployment of code. Kept as an unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: instance/src/main/java/org/apache/karaf/instance/core/internal/InstanceServiceImpl.java lines 613-629 (and doStart lines 489-557): javaOpts/name values are concatenated into a shell command string executed via ScriptUtils.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires an already-privileged shell user passing --java-opts to instance commands; it is command injection within the same privilege level rather than a trust-boundary crossing, so it was not selected.
Appears intentional in this design: role enforcement happens during authenticate() against the configured role property (lines 120-139); no bypass evidence found.

rejected_leads.lead: Dependency versions in poms (e.g., log4j 1.2.17, commons-beanutils 1.9.2, commons-fileupload 1.3.3).
rejected_leads.reason: Version-only observations without a source-level vulnerable code path in this snapshot; not pursued as a repository source vulnerability.

summary: Snapshot: Apache Karaf 4.3.0-SNAPSHOT (source-only tree; 1,660 files, all indexed; no src/test trees are present). I reviewed security-relevant code across obr, kar, http, shell (core/console/commands/ssh), management (JMX RBAC), jaas (login modules, keystore config), service/guard, features (download/XML), util (XML parsing, escaping, JAAS helper), config, log, audit, instance, webconsole and main. The strongest concrete security issue I found is a path-traversal / Zip-Slip in the OBR `obr:source` download-and-extract path: untrusted repository metadata supplies a source JAR URL (Resource.SOURCE_URI), and the extraction helper only rejects absolute JAR-entry paths, not `..` segments, so crafted entry names write outside the caller-specified folder. This matches a known Apache Karaf OBR path-traversal issue (CVE-2022-22932) that affects this version range, and the parallel KAR extractor in the same snapshot contains the missing `..`/`%2e%2e` guard, corroborating the intended validation. I also found an anomalous inverted null-check in Karaf's HTTP proxy servlet; it appears to be a genuine defect but I could not justify a concrete security impact for it, so it is recorded only as a rejected lead. No runtime, build, or exploit testing was performed.
